exam_questions.statement:
A student is finding the value of an unknown mass, $M$, of a fixed load by balancing it against a range of known masses on a metre rule. The rule rests on a pivot (balanced on a knife-edge) at its 50.0 cm mark. The load of unknown mass $M$ is fixed at the 5.0 cm position on the rule. A known mass $m$ is placed on the rule and its position is adjusted until the rule is exactly balanced; the distance $x$ (in cm), measured from the 50.0 cm balance point to the centre of mass $m$, is then recorded.

The student's results are:

| mass $m$/g | distance $x$/cm |
|---|---|
|60|37.4|
|70|31.9|
|80| (to be found) |
|90| (to be found) |
|100|22.7|

Close-up scale diagrams of the balanced rule show that, measuring to the centre of the mass: when $m=80\,\text{g}$ the mass sits at the 77.9 cm mark on the rule, and when $m=90\,\text{g}$ the mass sits at the 75.5 cm mark.

(a) (i) Use these two readings to find the distance $x$ (measured from the 50.0 cm balance point) for $m=80\,\text{g}$ and $m=90\,\text{g}$, and complete the table. [2]
(ii) Calculate $1/x$ for each value of $x$ in the table, giving your answers to 3 decimal places. [2]
(b) (i) A graph of mass $m$ (vertical axis) against $1/x$ (horizontal axis) is plotted using the five data points. Describe the shape/feature of this graph and how the best straight line should be drawn through the points. [2]
(ii) Calculate the gradient of the best-fit line through the plotted points, showing clearly how you obtained it. [2]
(c) Calculate the value of the unknown load of mass $M$, using the equation $M=\dfrac{\text{gradient}}{45}$. [1]
(d) This method of finding unknown masses is unsuitable for very small or very large masses. Suggest a reason for either of these. [1]
(Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences GCSE, Paper 61 Q6, May 2013)
exam_questions.answer:
(a)(i) $x=27.9\,\text{cm}$ (for 80 g); $x=25.5\,\text{cm}$ (for 90 g).
(ii) $1/x$ (cm$^{-1}$, 3 d.p.): 60 g$\to$0.027, 70 g$\to$0.031, 80 g$\to$0.036, 90 g$\to$0.039, 100 g$\to$0.044.
(b)(i) The points lie close to a straight line that passes through (or very close to) the origin, with the points scattered roughly evenly either side of the drawn line.
(ii) gradient $\approx 2300$–$2350\,\text{g}\,\text{cm}$ (taking $\approx 2350\,\text{g}\,\text{cm}$).
(c) $M=\dfrac{2350}{45}\approx 52\,\text{g}$ (accept any value found consistently from a sensible best-fit line, roughly in the range 45–55 g).
(d) e.g. for a very small $M$, the balancing distance $x$ would have to be very small (close to the pivot), making it hard to measure precisely (large percentage error); for a very large $M$, $x$ would have to be very large — possibly larger than the rule allows, or would need masses $m$ bigger than those available.
exam_questions.full_solution:
Taking moments about the pivot (the 50.0 cm mark): the unknown load $M$ is 45 cm from the pivot (50.0-5.0=45), so its moment is $45M$. The known mass $m$ is a distance $x$ from the pivot, so its moment is $mx$. Balancing moments: $45M=mx$, i.e. $m=\dfrac{45M}{x}=45M\times\dfrac{1}{x}$. This is exactly a straight line through the origin if $m$ is plotted against $1/x$, of gradient $45M$ — which is why $M=\text{gradient}/45$.

(a)(i) Reading the position of the mass directly off the rule: for 80 g the mass is at the 77.9 cm mark, so $x=77.9-50.0=27.9\,\text{cm}$. For 90 g the mass is at the 75.5 cm mark, so $x=75.5-50.0=25.5\,\text{cm}$.
Check for consistency: $m\times x$ should be roughly constant ($=45M$) for every row — $60\times37.4=2244$, $70\times31.9=2233$, $80\times27.9=2232$, $90\times25.5=2295$, $100\times22.7=2270$ (all g·cm). These cluster around 2230–2295, confirming the two new readings are consistent with the rest of the (slightly scattered, as real experimental data always is) data set.
(ii) $1/x$: $1/37.4=0.0267\ldots\to0.027$; $1/31.9=0.03135\ldots\to0.031$; $1/27.9=0.03584\ldots\to0.036$; $1/25.5=0.03922\ldots\to0.039$; $1/22.7=0.04405\ldots\to0.044$ (all to 3 d.p.).
(b)(i) Since $m=45M\times(1/x)$ is a direct proportionality (no constant term), the five plotted points should lie close to a straight line that passes through the origin; the best-fit line is drawn so that the points are as close as possible to it, with roughly equal numbers of points above and below the line.
(ii) Draw the best-fit straight line and use a large triangle between two well-separated points on it. Because the points lie very close to the line, two points near its ends give a good value, for example $(0.027,60)$ and $(0.044,100)$: gradient $=\dfrac{100-60}{0.044-0.027}=\dfrac{40}{0.017}\approx2350\,\text{g cm}$. We take gradient $\approx2350\,\text{g cm}$.
(c) $M=\dfrac{\text{gradient}}{45}=\dfrac{2350}{45}\approx52.2\,\text{g}$, i.e. $M\approx52\,\text{g}$. (Because of the scatter in the raw data, a value anywhere from about 45 g to 55 g should be accepted, depending exactly how the best-fit line was drawn.)
(d) If $M$ were very small, then (from $x=45M/m$) the balance distance $x$ would be very small — close to the pivot — so a given reading error in $x$ becomes a very large percentage error, making $M$ hard to determine accurately. If $M$ were very large, $x=45M/m$ would need to be very large for any reasonably-sized $m$, which could require $x$ to extend beyond the usable length of the rule, or require known masses larger than those available in the set, making the method impractical.
mark_scheme: B1 1/x values correct to 3 d.p. for at least 3 of the 5 rows
B1 straight line graph through/near the origin
B1 points scattered reasonably either side of the drawn best-fit line
M1 gradient found using a large triangle / two well-separated points on the line (method shown)
A1 gradient value in the range ≈2200–2400 g cm (e.g. ≈2350 g cm)
B1 M = gradient/45, giving M in the range ≈45–55 g (e.g. ≈52 g)
B1 valid reason given for small-M or large-M limitation (e.g. x too small to measure accurately, or x/masses needed exceed what is available)

exam_questions.statement:
Figure 2.1 shows a simple a.c. generator: a rectangular coil of wire is mounted so that it can spin between the curved poles of a permanent magnet (N pole on the left, S pole on the right). The ends of the coil are connected, via slip rings and brushes, to an a.c. voltmeter which displays the alternating voltage produced as the coil spins.

(a) (i) The coil is now made to spin in the opposite direction to the one shown in Figure 2.1. What difference, if any, would be shown on the voltmeter reading? [1]
(ii) State two ways in which the size of the induced voltage can be increased. [2]
(b) In a power station there are several large generators. Explain why transformers are needed between the power transmission cables from the power station and the cables supplying homes. [2]
(Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences GCSE, Paper 32 Q6, Nov 2012)
exam_questions.answer:
(a)(i) No difference: the voltmeter reading stays the same (same size and frequency of voltage). (The alternating voltage is reversed in direction at each instant, but an a.c. voltmeter does not show this.)
(ii) Any two of: spin the coil faster; increase the number of turns on the coil; use a stronger magnet; add a soft-iron core inside the coil.
(b) A step-up transformer raises the voltage (and so lowers the current) for transmission, cutting I²R power losses in the cables; a step-down transformer is then needed to reduce this high voltage to a safe, usable level for homes.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a)(i) Reversing the direction of spin reverses the direction in which each side of the coil cuts the magnetic field lines, so at every instant the induced e.m.f. is in the opposite direction to before: the alternating voltage is simply 'flipped' (reversed in phase). However, the coil still spins at the same speed in the same field with the same number of turns, so the size (peak value) and frequency of the alternating voltage are unchanged. An a.c. voltmeter shows the size of the alternating voltage, not its direction at each instant, so its reading shows no difference.
(a)(ii) The size (peak value) of the induced e.m.f. in a generator increases if you: rotate the coil faster (greater rate of change of flux); increase the number of turns on the coil (more turns each contribute an e.m.f., which add together); use a stronger magnet (greater magnetic flux density); or add a soft-iron core to concentrate/strengthen the field through the coil. Any two of these are acceptable.
(b) Power stations generate electrical energy, which must be transmitted long distances along cables to reach homes. For a given amount of power transmitted, $P=VI$, so the higher the transmission voltage $V$, the smaller the current $I$ needed. Since the power wasted as heat in the cables is $I^2R$, a smaller current means much smaller power loss (and allows thinner, cheaper cables to be used) — so a step-up transformer is used at the power station to raise the voltage to a very high value for transmission. However, such a high voltage is far too dangerous and impractical to supply directly to homes, so a step-down transformer is used near the point of use to reduce the voltage back down to a safe, standard domestic supply voltage. Since transformers only work with alternating current, and each one is needed to change the voltage at its own stage, transformers are essential at both ends of the transmission system.
mark_scheme: B1 no difference in the reading (same size/magnitude of voltage, same frequency); allow 'voltage reversed in direction but same size'
B1 one valid way to increase induced voltage (e.g. spin faster / more turns / stronger magnet / add iron core)
B1 second valid way to increase induced voltage
M1 high transmission voltage → lower current → lower I²R power loss in cables (step-up transformer)
M1 step-down transformer needed to reduce the high transmission voltage to a safe level for homes

exam_questions.statement:
Figure 3.1 shows four swimmers diving into a pool at the start of a race.
(a) The swimmers start their race when they hear a loud, high-pitched sound from a loudspeaker.
(i) Describe how the loudspeaker causes the sound to travel through the air. Use the idea of compressions and rarefactions in your answer. You may describe a diagram if it helps your answer. [2]
(ii) Explain why sound travels at a different speed through water than through air. [2]
(b) Figure 3.2 shows the (regular, repeating) trace of a sound wave as it appears on an oscilloscope screen. Describe a second trace, from a sound that is louder than the one shown but has the same pitch. [2]
(c) Sound travels at 330 m/s in air. The loudspeaker produces a sound with a frequency of 200 Hz. Calculate the wavelength of this sound. State the formula that you use and show your working. [2]
(Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences GCSE, Paper 32 Q3 a,b,c, Nov 2012)
exam_questions.answer:
(a)(i) The loudspeaker cone vibrates back and forth, alternately compressing the air in front of it (compressions) and leaving regions where the air is more spread out (rarefactions); these travel outward as a longitudinal sound wave.
(ii) Sound travels faster in water than in air because water's particles are much more closely packed, so vibrations (and so energy) are passed from particle to particle more quickly.
(b) Same wavelength (same frequency/pitch) as the original trace, but with a greater amplitude (taller peaks and deeper troughs).
(c) $\lambda=v/f=330/200=1.65\,\text{m}$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a)(i) As the loudspeaker's cone vibrates, when it moves forward it pushes the nearby air particles closer together than normal — a region of compression (higher pressure); when it moves backward, those particles spread further apart than normal — a region of rarefaction (lower pressure). As the cone keeps vibrating, a regular pattern of alternating compressions and rarefactions moves outward through the air, away from the speaker; this is how the sound energy (not the air itself) travels as a longitudinal wave to reach the swimmers' ears.
(a)(ii) The speed at which a sound wave travels through a medium depends on how quickly one particle can pass its vibration on to the next. In water, the particles are much more closely packed (and more strongly bonded) than in air, so a vibrating particle collides with / pulls on its neighbour almost immediately, transferring the disturbance (and so the sound energy) onward much faster than in the widely-spaced, weakly-interacting particles of a gas like air. This is why the measured speed of sound in water (around 1500 m/s) is much greater than in air (330 m/s).
(b) Loudness of a sound depends on the amplitude of the wave (how much pressure varies above and below normal), while pitch depends on frequency (how many oscillations per second). Since the new sound is louder but has the same pitch as the original, its trace should show the same wavelength on the screen (same number of complete waves across the screen, i.e. unchanged frequency), but with a larger amplitude — taller peaks and correspondingly deeper troughs than the original trace.
(c) Using the wave equation $v=f\lambda$: $\lambda=\dfrac{v}{f}=\dfrac{330\,\text{m/s}}{200\,\text{Hz}}=1.65\,\text{m}$.
mark_scheme: B1 cone/diaphragm vibrates back and forth
B1 compressions = particles pushed together/higher pressure; rarefactions = particles spread apart/lower pressure, travelling outward as a longitudinal wave
B1 particles in water are closer together / more densely packed than in air
B1 vibrations/energy passed between particles more quickly in water → greater speed
B1 same wavelength/frequency as original trace
B1 greater amplitude (taller peaks/deeper troughs) than original trace
B1 correct formula v = fλ (or λ = v/f) stated
B1 correct substitution and answer: λ = 1.65 m

exam_questions.statement:
(a) A resistor of 1200 Ω is connected in parallel with another resistor of 2400 Ω. Calculate the combined resistance of these two resistors. State the formula that you use and show your working. [3]
(b) Torches (flashlights) are usually powered by electrical cells. They can also be powered by energy from the Sun (solar energy). Solar energy is a renewable energy resource.
(i) Sort the following energy resources into renewable and non-renewable: coal, geothermal, hydroelectric, natural gas, oil, tidal, wave, wind. [1]
(ii) Name the process that releases energy within the Sun. [1]
(iii) Energy is transferred from the Sun to the Earth by radiation. Explain why energy cannot be transferred from the Sun to the Earth by conduction. [1]
(c) Figure 4.1 shows a torch that works without electrical cells. To use the torch it is first shaken for 40 seconds. This moves a powerful magnet backwards and forwards inside a large coil of wire inside the torch (the magnet can move between two points, X and Y), charging an electric storage device. Explain why shaking the torch produces an electric current. [4]
(Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences GCSE, Paper 32 Q7, May 2013)
exam_questions.answer:
(a) $R=800\,\Omega$.
(b)(i) Renewable: geothermal, hydroelectric, tidal, wave, wind. Non-renewable: coal, natural gas, oil.
(ii) Nuclear fusion.
(iii) Conduction needs a medium of particles in contact; there is a vacuum (no particles) between the Sun and the Earth, so conduction cannot occur.
(c) Shaking moves the magnet through the coil, continuously changing the magnetic flux linking the coil; by electromagnetic induction this changing flux induces an e.m.f. in the coil; since the coil is part of a complete circuit, the induced e.m.f. drives an induced current, which charges the storage device.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) For resistors in parallel, $\dfrac{1}{R}=\dfrac{1}{R_1}+\dfrac{1}{R_2}=\dfrac{1}{1200}+\dfrac{1}{2400}=\dfrac{2}{2400}+\dfrac{1}{2400}=\dfrac{3}{2400}=\dfrac{1}{800}$, so $R=800\,\Omega$. (Check: parallel resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistor — 800 Ω < 1200 Ω ✓.)
(b)(i) Renewable resources are naturally replenished on a human timescale: geothermal (heat from the Earth's interior), hydroelectric (flowing/falling water), tidal, wave and wind. Non-renewable (fossil fuel) resources, which take millions of years to form and are being used up faster than they form, are: coal, natural gas and oil.
(ii) The Sun releases energy by nuclear fusion — hydrogen nuclei fuse together under immense pressure and temperature to form helium nuclei, releasing a huge amount of energy in the process.
(iii) Conduction is the transfer of (vibrational/kinetic) energy directly between neighbouring particles that are in contact with one another — it therefore needs a material medium (solid, liquid or gas) to take place. Between the Sun and the Earth is (essentially) a vacuum, containing no particles, so there is nothing for the energy to be passed between — conduction (and convection, which also needs a fluid medium) is impossible, leaving radiation (electromagnetic waves, which can travel through empty space) as the only way the energy can cross the gap.
(c) Shaking the torch makes the permanent magnet move repeatedly back and forth through the large coil of wire. As the magnet moves, the magnetic flux (the amount of magnetic field) passing through/linking the coil is continually changing. By the principle of electromagnetic induction (Faraday's law), whenever the magnetic flux linking a coil changes, an e.m.f. (voltage) is induced in that coil. Since the coil forms part of a complete electrical circuit (connected to the storage device), this induced e.m.f. drives an induced current around the circuit, charging the storage device; as the magnet changes direction between X and Y, the induced current also reverses direction each time (i.e. an alternating current is produced).
mark_scheme: M1 correct parallel-resistance formula used (1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2)
A1 correct combination giving 1/R = 1/800
A1 final answer R = 800 Ω
B1 all 8 resources correctly sorted into renewable/non-renewable
B1 (nuclear) fusion
B1 vacuum between Sun and Earth has no particles, so there is nothing for conduction to occur through
B1 magnet moves relative to / through the coil
B1 this changes the magnetic flux/field linking the coil
B1 a changing flux induces an e.m.f./voltage in the coil (electromagnetic induction)
B1 the circuit is complete, so the induced e.m.f. drives a current, charging the storage device

exam_questions.statement:
(a) An elephant of mass 5000 kg exerts a constant force of 1400 N to push a tree trunk along at a steady speed of 1.5 m/s.
(i) Calculate the work done by the elephant when the tree trunk moves 10 m. State the formula that you use and show your working. [2]
(ii) Calculate the kinetic energy of the elephant when it is moving at 1.5 m/s. State the formula that you use and show your working. [2]
(b) The elephant has a weight of 50000 N and stands with all four feet in contact with the ground. Each foot of the elephant has an area of 0.2 m². Calculate the pressure exerted by the elephant on the ground. State the formula that you use and show your working. [2]
(c) The volume of the elephant is 5 m³. Its mass is 5000 kg. Calculate the density of the elephant. State the formula that you use and show your working. [2]
(Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences GCSE, Paper 32 Q2, May 2013)
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a)(i) Work done $W=Fd=1400\,\text{N}\times10\,\text{m}=14000\,\text{J}$. (The steady speed means there is no change in kinetic energy, so all this work goes into overcoming friction/resistance from the trunk — but the question only asks for work done, which is simply force × distance moved in the direction of the force.)
(ii) Kinetic energy $KE=\frac12mv^2=0.5\times5000\,\text{kg}\times(1.5\,\text{m/s})^2=0.5\times5000\times2.25=5625\,\text{J}$.
(b) The elephant's weight is shared between 4 feet, each of area $0.2\,\text{m}^2$, so the total contact area is $4\times0.2=0.8\,\text{m}^2$. Pressure $P=\dfrac{F}{A}=\dfrac{50000\,\text{N}}{0.8\,\text{m}^2}=62500\,\text{Pa}$ (a reasonable, large value, consistent with an elephant's weight spread over a fairly small total foot area).
(c) Density $\rho=\dfrac{m}{V}=\dfrac{5000\,\text{kg}}{5\,\text{m}^3}=1000\,\text{kg/m}^3$ (very close to the density of water, which is physically sensible for a large animal that is mostly water/tissue).
mark_scheme: M1 W = Fd used
M1 KE = ½mv² used
A1 KE = 5625 J
M1 total area = 4 × 0.2 = 0.8 m² and P = F/A used
M1 ρ = m/V used
A1 ρ = 1000 kg/m³

exam_questions.statement:
Figure 6.1 shows a solar-powered golf cart used to carry golfers around a golf course.
(a) As the cart moves around the course, its motion is measured. Figure 6.2 is a distance/time graph for a small part of the journey: the graph passes through the points A(0 s, 0 m), B(10 s, 10 m), C(20 s, 60 m), D(30 s, 68 m), E(40 s, 68 m) and F(60 s, 80 m), each pair of consecutive points joined by a straight line.
(i) Show that the speed of the cart between B and C is 5 m/s. Show your working. [1]
(ii) The mass of the cart is 400 kg. Calculate the kinetic energy of the cart between B and C. State the formula that you use, show your working and state the unit of your answer. [2]
(iii) Describe the motion of the cart between D and E. [1]
(iv) Later in the journey, the cart accelerates from 1 m/s to 3 m/s in 5 seconds. Calculate the acceleration of the cart. State the formula that you use, show your working and state the unit of your answer. [2]
(b) (i) During the cart's journey, the temperature of the air inside the tyres increases by 15°C, while the volume of the air in the tyre remains the same. Explain, in terms of particles, why the pressure of the air in the tyre increases when this happens. [1]
(ii) Sometimes the golfer's hands begin to sweat. Explain, in terms of particles, how sweating cools his hands by evaporation. [2]
(iii) During this evaporation, water changes state from liquid to gas. Describe, in terms of the arrangement, spacing and movement of the particles, the difference between a liquid and a gas. [2]
(Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences GCSE, Paper 33 Q9, Nov 2013)
exam_questions.answer:
(a)(i) speed $=\dfrac{60-10}{20-10}=5\,\text{m/s}$.
(ii) $KE=5000\,\text{J}$.
(iii) The cart is stationary (at rest) between D and E.
(iv) $a=0.4\,\text{m/s}^2$.
(b)(i) Faster-moving particles hit the tyre walls more often and harder, increasing pressure.
(ii) The most energetic water molecules evaporate, lowering the average kinetic energy (temperature) of the remaining sweat and removing heat energy from the skin.
(iii) Liquid: particles close together, randomly arranged, able to move/slide past each other. Gas: particles far apart, moving fast and randomly in all directions, with almost no forces between them.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a)(i) From the graph, between B (10 s, 10 m) and C (20 s, 60 m) the cart travels $60-10=50\,\text{m}$ in a time of $20-10=10\,\text{s}$. Speed $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}=\dfrac{50}{10}=5\,\text{m/s}$, as required.
(ii) Kinetic energy $KE=\frac12mv^2=0.5\times400\,\text{kg}\times(5\,\text{m/s})^2=0.5\times400\times25=5000\,\text{J}$.
(iii) Between D (30 s, 68 m) and E (40 s, 68 m) the distance travelled does not change (it stays at 68 m) even though 10 seconds pass, so the graph is a horizontal (flat) line here — the cart is not moving at all; it is stationary/at rest for this part of the journey.
(iv) Acceleration $a=\dfrac{v-u}{t}=\dfrac{3-1}{5}=\dfrac{2}{5}=0.4\,\text{m/s}^2$.
(b)(i) At constant volume, raising the temperature gives the air particles inside the tyre more kinetic energy, so they move faster (higher average speed). Faster particles collide with the inside walls of the tyre both more frequently and with a greater force per collision (greater momentum change each time). Since pressure is the total force exerted per unit area by these collisions, both effects together increase the pressure of the air in the tyre.
(ii) Sweat is a liquid made of water molecules with a range of different kinetic energies (speeds). Evaporation happens when the most energetic molecules at the surface have enough kinetic energy to escape into the air as vapour, even below boiling point. Because it is specifically the highest-energy particles that leave, the particles left behind in the liquid sweat have a lower average kinetic energy than before — and since temperature is a measure of average particle kinetic energy, the remaining sweat (and the skin in contact with it) is cooled. In other words, the energy needed to evaporate the escaping molecules (the latent heat of vaporisation) is drawn from the skin, cooling it down.
(iii) In a liquid, the particles are close together (touching their neighbours, with very little empty space between them), arranged randomly rather than in a fixed pattern, and are free to move around and slide past one another — this is why a liquid can flow and takes the shape of its container, while still having a fixed volume. In a gas, the particles are very much further apart (large, mostly empty spaces between them), with negligible forces between them, and move rapidly and completely randomly in all directions, constantly colliding with each other and with the walls of their container — this is why a gas has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume, and always expands to fill whatever container it is in.
mark_scheme: B1 speed = (60−10)/(20−10) = 5 m/s shown using graph values
M1 KE = ½mv² used
A1 KE = 5000 J
B1 cart is stationary/at rest (zero speed) between D and E
M1 a = (v−u)/t used
A1 a = 0.4 m/s²
B1 particles move faster/have more KE, so collide with tyre walls more often and/or harder, increasing pressure
B1 most energetic particles escape/evaporate
B1 this lowers the average KE/temperature of the remaining liquid, cooling the skin (energy taken from skin)
B1 liquid: particles close together, randomly arranged, able to move/slide past each other
B1 gas: particles far apart, move fast and randomly in all directions, fill their container

exam_questions.statement:
(a) Figure 7.1 shows a circuit used to measure the current passing through a fixed resistor when the voltage across it is changed: a battery is connected in series with a variable resistor (rheostat) and an ammeter; the ammeter is connected to the fixed resistor, and a voltmeter is connected in parallel across the fixed resistor. Complete the following sentences using suitable words.
'When the voltage across the resistor is reduced, the current through the resistor ______.'
'When the voltage of the supply is reduced, the voltage across the resistor ______.' [1]
(b) The resistance of a piece of wire depends on a number of variables such as the temperature of the wire and the material from which it is made. State two other factors which affect the resistance of a piece of wire. [2]
(c) Figure 7.2 shows a circuit used to power a small motor: a battery is connected in series with an ammeter and the motor M, and a voltmeter is connected in parallel across the motor. The voltage across the motor is 3 V. The current through the motor is 0.6 A.
(i) Calculate the power input to the motor. State the formula that you use, show your working and state the unit of your answer. [2]
(ii) The motor is able to lift a load of 40 N through 1.2 m in 36 seconds. Calculate the power output of the motor. State the formula that you use, show your working and state the unit of your answer. [3]
(iii) Explain why there is a difference between your answers to (i) and (ii). [1]
(iv) Calculate the efficiency of the motor. Show your working. [2]
(d) An electric current in a wire is a flow of electrons. β (beta) radiation also consists of electrons.
(i) State the sign of the charge on an electron. [1]
(ii) α (alpha) radiation moves in the opposite direction to β radiation in an electric field. γ (gamma) radiation passes through an electric field without deviation. Explain these two statements. [2]
(Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences GCSE, Paper 33 Q3, Nov 2013)
exam_questions.answer:
(a) decreases; decreases.
(b) Any two of: the length of the wire; the cross-sectional area (thickness) of the wire.
(c)(i) $P=1.8\,\text{W}$.
(ii) $P\approx1.33\,\text{W}$.
(iii) The motor is not 100% efficient — some electrical energy input is wasted (e.g. as heat/sound) rather than converted to useful mechanical output.
(iv) efficiency $\approx74\%$.
(d)(i) Negative.
(ii) β particles (electrons) are negative and α particles are positive, so opposite charges are deflected in opposite directions by the field; γ radiation is uncharged electromagnetic radiation, so it experiences no force in an electric field and is not deflected.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) By Ohm's law $V=IR$ with $R$ constant: if the voltage across the resistor is reduced, the current through it must also fall (they are directly proportional) — so the current decreases. Likewise, if the supply voltage is reduced, with the circuit's proportions unchanged the share of voltage appearing across the fixed resistor is also reduced — so the voltage across the resistor decreases.
(b) Resistance of a wire also depends on its length (a longer wire has more resistance, since the charge carriers have further to travel and more collisions occur) and its cross-sectional area/thickness (a thinner wire has more resistance, since there is less cross-section for current to flow through, similar to a narrower pipe restricting water flow more).
(c)(i) Electrical power input $P=VI=3\,\text{V}\times0.6\,\text{A}=1.8\,\text{W}$.
(ii) Useful work done by the motor $=Fd=40\,\text{N}\times1.2\,\text{m}=48\,\text{J}$. Power output $=\dfrac{\text{work done}}{\text{time taken}}=\dfrac{48\,\text{J}}{36\,\text{s}}=1.333\ldots\approx1.33\,\text{W}$.
(iii) The power output (≈1.33 W) is less than the power input (1.8 W) because real motors are never perfectly (100%) efficient — some of the electrical energy supplied is converted into unwanted forms of energy, particularly heat (due to the electrical resistance of the motor's coils and friction in its bearings) and some sound, rather than all of it being converted into useful mechanical (lifting) work.
(iv) Efficiency $=\dfrac{\text{useful output power}}{\text{input power}}\times100\%=\dfrac{1.333}{1.8}\times100\%\approx74.1\%$ — i.e. about 74% (which is a sensible efficiency for a small real electric motor, well below 100% as expected).
(d)(i) An electric current is a flow of electrons, and electrons carry a negative charge.
(ii) In an electric field, charged particles experience a force and are deflected towards the oppositely-charged plate. β radiation consists of electrons, which are negatively charged, so β particles are deflected towards the positive plate. α radiation consists of helium nuclei, which are positively charged, so α particles are deflected towards the negative plate — i.e. in the opposite direction to β, because the two types of radiation carry opposite signs of charge. γ radiation, however, is a form of electromagnetic radiation (high-energy photons) and carries no electric charge at all, so it experiences no electric force and travels straight through an electric field without any deviation.
mark_scheme: B1 both blanks correctly completed: decreases; decreases
B1 length of wire
B1 cross-sectional area/thickness of wire
M1 P = VI used
M1 work done = Fd = 48 J
M1 power = work/time used
A1 power output ≈ 1.33 W
B1 motor not 100% efficient — energy wasted as heat/sound rather than all converted to useful mechanical output
M1 efficiency = output power/input power × 100% used
A1 efficiency ≈ 74%
B1 negative
B1 α positive and β negative, so opposite charges deflected in opposite directions
B1 γ is uncharged electromagnetic radiation, so experiences no force/no deviation in the field

exam_questions.statement:
(a) Figure 8.1 shows two bar magnets, A and B. Magnet B hangs freely by a string from a wooden stand, with its N pole on the left and its S pole on the right (facing towards A). Magnet A, positioned to the right of B, has its S pole on the left (its leading edge, facing towards B) and its N pole on the right; magnet A is moved towards magnet B (i.e. to the left, towards B).
(i) Describe and explain what happens to magnet B as magnet A is moved towards it. [1]
(ii) Magnet A is replaced by a piece of unmagnetised iron, C (the same size/shape, moved towards B in the same way). Predict what happens as the unmagnetised iron C is moved towards B. Explain your prediction. [2]
(b) Figure 8.2 shows two plastic balls, X and Y, each hanging from its own thread (Y from a wooden stand, X held near Y on a thread by a person's hand); the two threads are shown tilted towards each other, i.e. the balls are attracted together. Both balls are electrically charged. Ball Y is negatively charged.
(i) State the charge on ball X. Give a reason for your answer. [1]
(ii) Describe and explain how ball Y could have been given a negative charge. [2]
(iii) There is an electric field between ball X and ball Y. State what happens to an electric charge placed in this field. [1]
(c) The mass of ball X is 3.97 g ($3.97\times10^{-3}\,\text{kg}$). The volume of ball X is 4.17 cm³ ($4.17\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3$). Calculate the density of the plastic used to make ball X. State the formula that you use and show your working. State the units of your answer. [3]
(Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences GCSE, Paper 33 Q5, May 2014)
exam_questions.answer:
(a)(i) Magnet B is repelled — it swings away from magnet A — because A's leading (S) pole faces B's near (S) pole, and like poles repel.
(ii) The unmagnetised iron C is attracted to B (B swings towards C): B's S pole induces an opposite (N) magnetic pole in the near end of the (magnetic but unmagnetised) iron, and induced magnetism is always attractive.
(b)(i) Positive — the balls are attracted to one another (threads lean together), and only unlike charges attract.
(ii) Ball Y was charged by friction (rubbing against another material); rubbing transfers electrons between the two surfaces, and Y ends up with a surplus (excess) of electrons, giving it an overall negative charge.
(iii) It experiences an electric (electrostatic) force and is made to move/accelerate along the field — a positive charge towards Y, a negative charge towards X.
(c) $\rho\approx952\,\text{kg/m}^3$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a)(i) As magnet A approaches magnet B, it is A's leading (left-hand) pole that gets closer to B — and A's leading pole is S. The pole of B facing A (its right-hand pole) is also S. Because like magnetic poles (S and S) repel one another, a repulsive force pushes magnet B away from magnet A; since B hangs freely on a string, it swings away from A as A approaches.
(ii) Unlike a permanent magnet, unmagnetised iron has no poles of its own — but it is still a magnetic material, so it becomes magnetised by induction whenever it is brought near a magnet. As iron C approaches magnet B, the magnetic field from B's S pole induces an opposite magnetic pole (an N pole) at the near end of C. Because induced magnetism always produces an attractive interaction with the inducing magnet (regardless of which pole of the permanent magnet is nearest), the induced N pole of C is attracted to the S pole of B — so, unlike the repulsion seen with magnet A, iron C and magnet B attract each other, and B swings towards C.
(b)(i) The figure shows the two balls' threads both tilted towards each other, meaning the balls are pulled towards one another — i.e. they attract. Since electric charges only attract when they are of opposite sign, and ball Y is negative, ball X must carry a positive charge.
(ii) The most likely way to charge an object like ball Y (an insulator) is by friction: rubbing it against a different material (e.g. a cloth) causes electrons to be transferred from one surface to the other, because the two materials hold on to electrons with different strengths. If, during this rubbing, electrons are transferred onto ball Y (rather than away from it), Y ends up with more electrons than protons — i.e. an overall surplus (excess) of negative charge — making it negatively charged.
(iii) An electric field exerts a force on any electric charge placed within it, causing that charge to experience an electrostatic force and so to accelerate/move in response. The direction depends on the sign of the charge: since the field points from the positive ball (X) towards the negative ball (Y), a positive test charge placed in the field would be pushed in the direction of the field (from X towards Y), whereas a negative test charge would be pushed in the opposite direction (from Y towards X).
(c) Density $\rho=\dfrac{m}{V}=\dfrac{3.97\times10^{-3}\,\text{kg}}{4.17\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3}\approx952\,\text{kg/m}^3$ (this is a reasonable density for a solid plastic, somewhat less than that of water).
mark_scheme: B1 magnet B repelled/swings away, because the two facing (S) poles are the same (like poles repel)
B1 iron C becomes magnetised by induction, with its near end taking the opposite polarity to B's facing pole
B1 induced poles always attract (unlike the repulsion with magnet A), so B swings towards C
B1 ball X is positive, because the balls attract and only unlike charges attract
B1 ball Y charged by friction/rubbing with another material
B1 electrons transferred onto Y, giving it a surplus of electrons (negative charge)
B1 a charge placed in the field experiences an electric force and accelerates/moves along the field (direction depending on its sign)
M1 ρ = m/V used
M1 correct substitution of given values
A1 ρ ≈ 952 kg/m³ with correct unit
